entities.evidence: אֱלֹהִים is the subject of the singular verb וַיַּרְא. The Creator introduced in Genesis 1:1 sees that the work is good.

review.translation: [and to rule|0] [over the day|1] [and over the night|2], [and to distinguish|3] [between|4] [the light|5] [and|6] [the darkness|7]. [And|8] [God|9] [saw|8] [that|10] {it was} [good|11].

analysis.evidence: בַּיּוֹם וּבַלַּיְלָה identifies day and night as the domains the lights govern. The parallel infinitive וּלֲהַבְדִּיל gives their further purpose, to separate light from darkness.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וְ and preposition לִ precede the Qal infinitive construct מְשֹׁל, which expresses purpose.
analysis.sense: rule over day and night, as the heavenly lights do

analysis.evidence: The verse pairs בַּיּוֹם with וּבַלַּיְלָה, “and by night,” then contrasts הָאוֹר, “the light,” with הַחֹשֶׁךְ, “the darkness.” Both pairings identify יוֹם as the daylight period.
analysis.morphology: Preposition בְּ with the definite article הַ, followed by a masculine singular absolute noun.
analysis.sense: daylight, the day as against night

draft.change: Link the occurrence to the existing Hebrew noun לַיְלָה at word index 0 and its sense the-hours-of-darkness.
draft.definition: Night is the period of darkness paired with day.
draft.evidence: Genesis 1:18 places night alongside day and distinguishes light from darkness. The current ליל article already cites this verse under “the hours of darkness.”

analysis.evidence: Genesis 1:18 pairs בַּיּוֹם “in the day” with וּבַלַּיְלָה “and in the night” as the two periods in which the lights rule. The following distinction between light and darkness identifies night as the dark period.
analysis.morphology: וּ is the conjunction “and.” בַ combines the preposition בְּ “in” with the definite article, which doubles the following ל. לַיְלָה is a masculine singular absolute noun.

draft.change: Add the Hebrew verb בָּדַל with its Hiphil sense of separating.
draft.definition: To separate one thing from another.
draft.evidence: In Gen.1.4, God separates light from darkness. The repeated בֵּין introduces each member of the pair.

analysis.evidence: וּלֲהַבְדִּיל parallels וְלִמְשֹׁל, giving a second purpose of the luminaries. בֵּין הָאוֹר וּבֵין הַחֹשֶׁךְ identifies the two things they separate, light and darkness.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וּ plus preposition לֲ plus Hiphil infinitive construct הַבְדִּיל.
analysis.sense: to separate one thing from another

analysis.evidence: After וּלֲהַבְדִּיל ‘and to distinguish’, the marked בֵּין introduces הָאוֹר ‘the light’. The matching וּבֵין introduces הַחֹשֶׁךְ ‘the darkness’, the second term of the distinction.
analysis.morphology: Preposition in the construct form בֵּין, without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In וּלֲהַבְדִּיל בֵּין הָאוֹר וּבֵין הַחֹשֶׁךְ, “and to separate the light from the darkness,” הָאוֹר names what is distinguished from הַחֹשֶׁךְ.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הָ־ prefixed to a common noun of common gender, singular absolute.

analysis.evidence: In וּלֲהַבְדִּיל בֵּין הָאוֹר וּבֵין הַחֹשֶׁךְ ‘and to distinguish the light from the darkness’, וּבֵין introduces הַחֹשֶׁךְ ‘the darkness’ as the second term of the distinction.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וּ־ ‘and’ prefixed to the preposition בֵּין, with no suffix.

analysis.evidence: In וּלֲהַבְדִּיל בֵּין הָאוֹר וּבֵין הַחֹשֶׁךְ, the lights separate light from darkness. The contrast with הָאוֹר and the preceding mention of day and night establish the physical sense.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הַ־ prefixed to a masculine singular absolute noun.

analysis.evidence: אֱלֹהִים is the subject of וַיַּרְא, and כִּי טוֹב states what God saw: that it was good.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־
analysis.sense: see or perceive that something is so

analysis.evidence: In וַיַּרְא אֱלֹהִים כִּי טוֹב, “God saw that it was good,” the third-person masculine singular verb וַיַּרְא agrees with אֱלֹהִים as its subject and identifies the creator as the one who saw.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, masculine plural absolute, with a singular referent.

draft.change: Clarify the existing Gen.3.6 citation under ki-that by identifying the role of the second כִּי.
draft.definition: After a verb of perception, כִּי introduces what is perceived.
draft.evidence: In Gen.3.6 the repeated כִּי introduces a second clause governed by וַתֵּרֶא, and the prefixed וְ coordinates it with the first.

analysis.evidence: In וַיַּרְא אֱלֹהִים כִּי טוֹב, כִּי introduces what God saw, “that it was good.”
analysis.morphology: Uninflected conjunction with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: Introduces the content of what is seen.

analysis.evidence: וַיַּרְא אֱלֹהִים כִּי טוֹב means “God saw that it was good.” טוֹב expresses God’s judgment on the arrangement just described, in which the lights govern day and night and separate light from darkness.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular absolute adjective, used predicatively.
